blogs.title: Keeping DuPont Factors in Sync: The Federal Circuit Demands a Consistent Scope of “Similarity”
blogs.description: The court’s core holding is methodological: once the Board found the parties’ services highly similar (indeed, legally identical in part) under DuPont factor two, it could not constrict the universe of “similar” goods/services under factor six to credit cards alone. This post unpacks the requirement to harmonize the scope of similarity across factors, why the Board’s narrower lens was a legal error, and how this alignment will reshape TTAB practice—especially in defining relevant markets and curating third‑party evidence.

blogs.title: How Much Third-Party Use Is Enough? Recalibrating “Crowded Field” Evidence After Juice Generation and Jack Wolfskin
blogs.description: The Board dismissed 42 Aspire-formative uses outside credit cards and deemed nine credit card uses insufficient to show weakness. The Federal Circuit didn’t bless nine as too few; it vacated because the field was defined too narrowly. This post revisits the qualitative and quantitative thresholds for showing commercial weakness, the kinds of third‑party use and registration evidence that matter, and practical tips for applicants and opposers in building a factor‑six record in financial services disputes.

blogs.title: Commercial Impression Is Not Static: Why Vacating Factor Six Forced a Do-Over on Factor One
blogs.description: By vacating the strength analysis, the court necessarily unsettled the comparison of ASPIRE versus ASPIRE BANK. This post explores the interdependence between mark strength (factor six) and commercial impression (factor one): how marketplace crowding can change what consumers notice, how much weight to give shared elements like “ASPIRE,” and why the Board must reconsider appearance, sound, connotation, and overall impression in light of any revised strength finding on remand.

blogs.title: Defining “Credit Card Services” After the ID Manual Deletion: Implications for Fintechs and Bank Partners
blogs.description: The Board had to construe “credit card services” post‑deletion from the ID Manual and read it broadly to include issuing cards, processing payments, authorization, account management, alerts, and credit score access. Combined with dictionary definitions of “banking” and “finance,” the Board deemed the parties’ services legally identical in part, and the Federal Circuit affirmed. This post analyzes the interpretive move, its significance for fintech‑bank arrangements, and drafting strategy for applicants who recite “banking and financing services” but believe their offerings are operationally distinct.

blogs.title: From Publication to Opposition: What Apex’s Path Teaches About Letters of Protest, ITUs, and the Limits of Examiner Approval
blogs.description: Apex cleared examination and publication despite a protest, only to lose at the TTAB and partly on appeal. This post examines the procedural trajectory: how letters of protest interface with examination, why initial approval is a thin reed compared to a full DuPont record in opposition, the standard of review (de novo for legal issues; substantial evidence for facts), and strategic lessons for intent‑to‑use applicants in high‑overlap industries like financial services.

blogs.title: “We Don’t Issue Credit Cards” Isn’t a Shield: Services Overlap in the Banking-as-a-Service Era
blogs.description: Apex argued it does not offer credit cards and that CC Serve partners with banks. The Board—and the Federal Circuit—focused on the recited services and marketplace realities: consumers may believe related financial services come from a single source, and co‑branding/servicing models don’t erase overlap. This post surveys how modern bank‑fintech ecosystems drive factor‑two findings of similarity, what evidence can narrow perceived overlap, and why applicants should tailor identifications with care.
